title: Dynamo: never refuse to add to the cart
dek: In 2007 a large online shop described the key-value store behind its shopping cart: accept every write, even when disks fail and networks split, and sort out conflicting versions later. Its toolbox of consistent hashing, quorums, vector clocks, hinted handoff and gossip became the standard kit for leaderless databases.

items: Dynamo picks availability over consistency: a write is accepted as long as a few nodes are reachable, and conflicting versions are merged afterwards.
Keys live on a hash ring and are copied to the next N nodes. With N = 3, a write waits for W = 2 copies and a read asks R = 2, so a read normally overlaps the latest write.
Vector clocks spot conflicting versions and the application merges them. For a cart that means keeping every item, so a deleted item can come back.

body.x: The paper: "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" by Giuseppe DeCandia and eight co-authors, SOSP 2007.

For a shop, a customer who can't add to the cart is a lost sale. The authors' requirement was that the cart keeps accepting writes while disks fail, network links flap or a whole data centre is lost. Databases of the time usually stopped accepting writes during such failures to stay consistent, which was exactly the wrong trade for a cart.
They also measured latency differently: not the average but the 99.9th percentile, so that the slowest one in a thousand requests, often from customers with the longest histories, was still fast.

items: Each node takes several positions on a ring of hash values, called virtual nodes, so load spreads evenly and a new node takes a little from many others instead of a lot from one.
A key's hash picks a point on the ring, and the next N distinct nodes clockwise store it.
Any node can take a request and pass it to the right ones: there is no leader and no master.

body.cap: With N = 3 the cart lives on B, C and D. When C is down the write still succeeds: E takes it with a hint and hands it back when C recovers. The quorum counts the first three healthy nodes, not always the same three, which the paper calls a sloppy quorum.

What it does

The fastest writes, accepted while even one copy is reachable, but a read may miss them
The fastest reads, but a write fails if any one copy is down

body.x: Because the quorum is sloppy, R + W > N makes reading the latest write likely, not certain, after failures. The conflicting versions that slip through are caught by vector clocks.
Conflicts: vector clocks, merged by the app

body.cap: Each version carries a vector clock: one counter per node that changed it. If one clock is at least as large in every entry, that version is newer and the other is discarded. If neither is, both go back to the application to merge.

body.x: Conflicts were rare in practice: over a day the authors measured, 99.94% of reads saw exactly one version.

The merge belongs to the application because only it knows what the data means. For a cart, keeping the union of items never loses an addition, at the cost that a removed item can reappear. Stores that merge with last write wins instead silently drop one of the two edits.

items: Hinted handoff covers short outages, as in the ring figure.
For longer ones, nodes compare their key ranges with Merkle trees, trees of hashes where equal roots mean equal data, so two nodes find the few keys that differ without sending everything.
Every second, each node gossips its view of membership with a random other node, so all nodes learn of joins and departures without a central list.

body.x: Dynamo itself stayed internal, but the paper became a recipe. Cassandra, Riak and Voldemort built on its ring, quorums and gossip, Cassandra with Bigtable's storage layout underneath. The lasting lesson is the trade itself: decide, for each kind of data, whether a refused write or a conflicting one is worse.

items: This is the design for the Key-value store problem: a hash ring with virtual nodes, N = 3 copies, tunable R and W, hinted handoff, gossip, and Merkle-tree repair.
Say what a conflict means for your data: a cart can merge two versions; a wallet balance cannot, so it needs a single leader or consensus instead.
Explain R + W > N with numbers, and what you give up with W = 1.
State latency goals as a high percentile (p99 or p99.9), not an average.

body.label: Go deeper: clocks that keep growing

body.x: Every node that coordinates a write adds an entry to the vector clock, so clocks could grow without limit. Dynamo stored a timestamp with each entry and dropped the oldest once a clock passed about ten entries. That can make two related versions look like a conflict, but the authors reported it never caused a problem in production.
